title: User-defined data types
overview: User-defined data types let a programmer represent a problem using meaningful structures instead of forcing everything into primitive types. At A2 you must know enumerated types, pointers, records and sets, understand why each is useful, and choose a suitable type for a scenario.
syllabusPoints: Define and use pointer types and dereferencing.
Define records, including nested records and records containing arrays.
Use sets and set operations and choose appropriate user-defined types.

definitions.definition: A programmer-defined type whose values come from a fixed list of named constants.
A variable that stores the address/reference of another data item.
A composite type grouping named fields that may have different data types.
An unordered collection of distinct values with operations such as union and intersection.
Follow a pointer to access the data stored at the referenced address.

sections.title: Enumerated types
content: Use an enumeration when only a fixed set of states is valid. It makes programs self-documenting and prevents meaningless values from being assigned.

examples.label: Cambridge-style pseudocode
examples.content:
TYPE TState = (Waiting, Running, Complete)
DECLARE State : TState
State <- Running

sections.title: Pointers
content: Pointers make dynamic structures possible because a node can refer to another node without the items needing to be contiguous in memory. The pointer stores an address; dereferencing accesses the target value. A null pointer represents 'no target'.

sections.title: Records
content: A record models one entity using several fields. Fields may have different types; records can contain arrays or other records, and arrays can contain records. This is ideal for students, products, employees and similar entities.

examples.label: Cambridge-style pseudocode
examples.content:
TYPE TStudent
  DECLARE Name : STRING
  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
  DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:3] OF INTEGER
ENDTYPE

sections.title: Sets
content: Sets are useful where membership matters but order and duplicates do not. Union combines members, intersection keeps common members, difference removes members of another set, and membership tests whether a value belongs to the set.

sections.title: Choosing a type
content: Base the choice on the data requirement: enum for fixed named choices; record for related fields; set for unique unordered membership; pointer for dynamic links. In an exam, justify the feature that fits the scenario rather than just defining the type.

examTips: Distinguish the pointer variable from the data it points to.
When justifying a type, tie the reason to the scenario.
A record is not an array: its fields can have different data types.
commonMistakes: Treating an enumeration as an indexed array.
Saying a pointer stores the record itself rather than an address/reference.
Assuming sets preserve insertion order or allow duplicate elements.
